props.title: Stromboli
props.initialSlug: War refugee adapts to life on volcanic island

sections.content: Stromboli marks a pivotal moment in both Roberto Rossellini's career and Italian Neorealism. The film stars Ingrid Bergman as Karin, a Lithuanian refugee who marries an Italian fisherman to escape a displaced persons camp, only to find herself trapped in an even more isolating existence on the volcanic island of Stromboli. The film emerged from the real-life affair between Rossellini and Bergman, which scandalized Hollywood, but produced a trilogy of masterpieces including Europa '51 (1952) and Journey to Italy (1954). These films bridge pure neorealism and modernist cinema, incorporating both documentary-style footage of village life and intense psychological portraiture.

sections.content: The volcanic island becomes both setting and metaphor, with Rossellini incorporating actual documentary footage of an eruption. This blending of fiction and reality was revolutionary, influencing directors like Antonioni (L'Avventura (1960)) and Godard (Contempt (1963)). Karin's isolation among the traditional villagers speaks to postwar displacement and alienation themes that would dominate European art cinema. The film's stark landscapes and spiritual crisis prefigure Red Desert (1964) and other modernist classics. SUBHEAD: The Rossellini-Bergman Collaboration

The personal and professional partnership between Rossellini and Bergman produced a radical shift in both their careers. Bergman, fresh from Hollywood hits like Casablanca (1942) and Notorious (1946), embraced a more naturalistic acting style. Rossellini moved beyond pure neorealism toward a cinema examining psychological and spiritual crises. Their collaboration influenced the emerging art house cinema of the 1950s and early 1960s, particularly directors like Antonioni and Bergman who explored feminine psychology and existential themes.
